title: SDK Env Mini-Course Curriculum (draft)
content:
Purpose:
This doc sketches a compact, hands-on mini-course (4 sessions) to onboard engineers to the Redwood SDKs and best-practice integration patterns. Target audience: backend/frontend engineers who need to safely add generation, streaming, embeddings, and function-calling into product flows in a single week.

Design principles:
- Low ceremony: examples run locally (docker or node/npm) and against a sandboxed Redwood dev key.
- Failure-first labs: intentionally trigger common integration problems (timeouts, truncated streams, rate-limits) so learners build resilient patterns.
- Measurable outcomes: short quiz + lab rubric per module.
- Reproducible: each lab includes a small repo, seed data, and a troubleshooting checklist.

Course overview (4 x 90 min live + self-paced components):
1) Module 0 — Prep & Quick Win (15–20 min prework + 90 min session)
   - Objective: get a minimal SDK call working end-to-end and understand auth/region basics.
   - Prework: install node, python, docker; grab sandbox API key; clone mini-course repo.
   - Live lab: call a text generation endpoint, print streaming tokens, capture first response.
   - Outputs: working repo with env.example, one successful generation log.

2) Module 1 — Robust Calls & Error Modes (90 min)
   - Objective: implement retry/backoff, idempotency keys, request timeouts, and graceful fallback to smaller variants.
   - Lab scenarios: transient 5xx, deterministic rate-limit 429, long-tail latency simulation.
   - Exercise: add exponential backoff with jitter, observe metrics and logs.
   - Checklist: retry limits, circuit-breaker thresholds, instrumentation hooks for latency buckets.

3) Module 2 — Streaming, Partial Responses, and UX (90 min)
   - Objective: integrate streaming tokens into a frontend demo and handle partial output/aborts.
   - Lab scenarios: client disconnects, truncated token train, function-calling mid-stream.
   - Exercise: implement incremental DOM updates and a server-side aggregator that commits the final text only after stream completion.

4) Module 3 — Embeddings, Reranking, and Cost Controls (90 min)
   - Objective: attach embeddings to a small docs index, implement similarity search, and add cost-budgeting knobs (max tokens, model selection).
   - Lab scenarios: batch-embedding vs single-call trade-offs, caching layer for frequently-seen queries.
   - Exercise: build a simple q/a layer that falls back to a static summary if embedding budget exceeded.

Assessment and rubric (per module):
- Quick quiz (5 mins): multiple-choice covering key configs.
- Lab rubric: Pass/Minor issues/Major issues. Criteria: reproducible run, correct handling of simulated failure, basic telemetry present.
- Passing rule: At least 3/4 modules with Pass or 1 Minor.

Materials delivered in repo:
- /labs/module-0 through /labs/module-3 (each contains README, Dockerfile, .env.example)
- /scripts/simulate-failures (node/python helpers to inject 429/5xx/timeouts)
- /templates/telemetry-snippets (opentelemetry + simple stdout options)
- /exercises/checklist.md (straight checklist for reviewers)

Sample quickstart (to be copied into README):
1) git clone https://github.com/redwood-inference/sdks-mini-course.git
2) cp labs/module-0/.env.example labs/module-0/.env && set REDWOOD_API_KEY to sandbox key
3) docker compose up --build (or npm run dev)
4) curl -X POST http://localhost:3000/generate -d '{"prompt":"Hello"}' -H 'Content-Type: application/json'

Failure-mode troubleshooting notes (short):
- 401 / auth errors: verify key and region prefix, check env var name, inspect server logs for redwood-auth header rejection.
- 429 spikes: confirm client is sending idempotency key if retrying; use per-route rate limit headers to backoff faster.
- Streaming disconnects: implement token buffer + ack; design UX to resume or show 'partial result'.
- Cost overruns: enforce max_tokens per request, apply adaptive sampling (lower model size for draft responses).

Instructor playbook (for 90-min sessions):
- 0–10 min: goals and prework check
- 10–40 min: guided walkthrough of starter code + first run
- 40–70 min: break into pairs, complete focused lab task
- 70–85 min: pairs present short findings, show one failure handled
- 85–90 min: 2-min quiz + next steps

Delivery variants (pick one per cohort):
- Self-serve: release as repo with videos and automated environment setup (CI-based check for lab completion).
- Instructor-led: 4 live sessions over a week with office hours.
- Embedded ramp: shipping a 2-hour condensed workshop for new hires.

Success metrics (post-rollout, 30 days):
- % of pilot engineers who complete course: target 60%
- % of SDK adopters with streaming implemented correctly in first PR: target 40%
- Mean time to first working generation (from onboarding to merged PR): target < 3 days
- Reduction in basic integration incidents (401/429/timeout misconfig): target 30% drop

Next steps (short-term):
- Convert module READMEs into step-by-step video clips (micro-videos 3–6 min).
- Add automated verification jobs that run the lab smoke tests and post status to GitHub PRs.
- Pair with Solutions Eng to pilot with 3 customer teams.

Open questions / decisions needed:
- Which sandbox key rotation policy do we teach? (short-lived vs long-lived dev keys)
- Do we include server-side SDK examples in Go and Java, or stick to node/python only?
- Ownership: who maintains the failure-simulation scripts (eng-tools or devx team)?

Appendix: quick checklist for PR reviewers when merging SDK integration:
- Environment variables documented and not leaking secrets
- Retry and backoff behaviour present for transient errors
- Streaming handled with a cancellation path and partial-result UX
- Embedding calls batched or cached to reduce unit costs
- Telemetry: at least one trace per request and token-level timing sample
